evaluation.positioning_hook: A ruthless daytime TV host who turned televised executions into ratings gold must confront the demon he unleashed when his final broadcast becomes a live reckoning with a murdered child’s ghost.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built for conversation: a notorious TV show, public executions, and a supernatural payoff. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant thriller because the material is dark, violent, and highly specific, but the hook is strong enough to travel.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening execution sequence and keeps sharpening as the show’s curse, the occult books, and the final live broadcast come into focus. The premise is easy to explain in one breath and the escalation is clean.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Vance is a strong lead because he’s charismatic, morally compromised, and actively complicit in the machine he built. Serena, Heather, and Shawn each have enough texture to matter, and the Vance/Serena fracture gives the story emotional weight beyond the genre engine.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s fusion of tabloid TV, state-sanctioned execution, documentary framing, and demonic possession is unusually confident and specific. The choice to make the horror inseparable from broadcast culture gives it a real point of view.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once the first deaths hit, the script keeps tightening the vise with each broadcast, each clue, and each failed attempt to stop the show. The final act is especially strong because it converts the central question into a live moral trap.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels fresh and immediately understandable: a TV personality who monetized public vengeance is forced to face the literal consequences of that bargain. The idea is novel but not abstract, which is the sweet spot for this kind of material.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The '90s daytime-TV ecosystem, congressional hearings, network pressure, crew hierarchy, and archival/documentary texture create a world that feels lived-in and story-generating. The studio itself becomes a pressure cooker with its own rules and rituals.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very distinct register: lurid, procedural, media-satirical, and genuinely eerie. The archival-footage framing and the dead-serious treatment of absurd spectacle give it a hard-to-copy identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the horror engine is a strong thematic spine about guilt, public appetite, and the cost of turning justice into entertainment. The Sasha/Willie material and Vance’s buried ethical failure give the story more emotional depth than the premise initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Vance/Serena/Shawn/Heather triangle-plus-one creates recurring friction, and the crew relationships give the studio a functioning ensemble texture. It’s still primarily Vance-driven, but the supporting dynamics are strong enough to generate scenes rather than just exposition.

lead_characters.name: Vance Carmichael
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, white, charismatic TV host and former prosecutor.
lead_characters.hook: A polished, weaponized charm machine who built his career by turning justice into spectacle and never once mistook himself for the villain. He is brilliant, vain, persuasive, and deeply self-justifying — the kind of man who can sell a moral lie so well that he starts believing it himself, right up until the lie starts killing people around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad — a man whose intelligence and self-delusion are the performance. It gives an actor the chance to play seduction, authority, panic, guilt, and spiritual collapse in one escalating arc.

lead_characters.name: Serena Carmichael
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, white, producer and Vance’s wife/ex-wife.
lead_characters.hook: Serena is the show’s conscience without being passive: she understands the machine, helped build it, and can still see the moral rot inside it. Her love for Vance is real, but it’s always in conflict with her need to stay honest about what he’s become, which makes her the emotional counterweight to his self-mythology.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Laura Linney in Ozark or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers real dramatic authority — the smart, wounded partner who can hold the frame opposite a larger-than-life lead. It offers a strong actor the chance to play intelligence, disappointment, and moral clarity without ever becoming a simple foil.

lead_characters.name: Shawn Moriarty
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, white, ex-director of the show.
lead_characters.hook: Shawn is the seasoned insider who knows exactly how the sausage gets made and has the scars to prove it. He starts as the pragmatic fixer and ends up as the guy who can no longer pretend the thing is merely a production problem, which gives him a dry, exhausted humanity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the vein of John Turturro in Severance or Jeffrey Wright in Westworld — the veteran who can carry institutional fatigue and quiet dread. It gives an actor a chance to play wit, complicity, and dawning horror in equal measure.

lead_characters.name: Heather Jenkins
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 20s to early 50s across the story, white, lighting technician and survivor.
lead_characters.hook: Heather is the working-class witness who starts as crew, becomes survivor, and gradually turns into the person most willing to name what everyone else is avoiding. Her burns and her steadiness make her the story’s most visible cost-of-doing-business character, and she carries the emotional truth of the studio’s damage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Kaitlyn Dever in Unbelievable a mix of vulnerability and steel — someone who can absorb trauma without disappearing. It offers a performer a vivid physical and emotional transformation, plus the authority of being the one who sees the truth first.

lead_characters.name: Willie Reams
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, white, condemned prisoner and occult vessel.
lead_characters.hook: Willie begins as the presumed monster and slowly reveals himself as something more unnerving: a man whose guilt, grief, and possible innocence have been swallowed by a larger force. By the end he becomes the story’s avenging intelligence, which makes him both victim and executioner.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-breaking, mythic role that gave Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men or Ralph Fiennes in Schindler’s List a terrifying stillness. It gives an actor a chance to play restraint, menace, sorrow, and supernatural authority without overexplaining any of it.

lead_characters.name: Sasha Reams
lead_characters.demographics: Female, child, white, deceased daughter appearing as a ghostly presence.
lead_characters.hook: Sasha is the story’s emotional and supernatural key: the innocent child whose image keeps returning as proof that the case was never morally settled. She is not just a ghost but the memory the show tried to bury, and her presence turns the finale from punishment into reckoning.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: For a child performer, this is the kind of haunting, iconic role that creates instant recognition — the performance territory of the child in The Sixth Sense or Room for a child actor with unusual stillness. It’s brief but unforgettable, with a strong visual and emotional imprint.

lead_characters.name: Brian
lead_characters.hook: Brian is the cocky, likable crew guy whose confidence masks how vulnerable he is to the studio’s corruption. He gives the show its first real sense of normal workplace banter before the horror turns him into one more casualty of the machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that lets an actor make a fast, memorable impression, like Shea Whigham in any number of prestige thrillers. It offers a clean comic-to-tragic turn and a death scene that becomes a major story beat.

lead_characters.name: Simon
lead_characters.hook: Simon is the blunt, skeptical technician who keeps trying to explain the impossible in technical terms until the impossible stops caring about his explanations. He brings a dry, skeptical energy that helps the horror feel grounded before it overwhelms him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a younger character actor a sharp, scene-stealing lane — the smart-ass technician who becomes the audience surrogate. It’s a good showcase for timing, disbelief, and escalating terror.

lead_characters.name: Jesse
lead_characters.hook: Jesse is the gifted audio guy whose sensitivity to the signal makes him the first person to hear the curse before anyone else can see it. He’s gentle, competent, and doomed, which makes his death feel like the loss of the one person actually doing the job right.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a tragic, memorable arc in the mold of Anton Yelchin-style sensitivity or a young character actor in a prestige horror piece. It offers a clean emotional hook and a technically specific performance lane.

lead_characters.name: Richard Hines
lead_characters.hook: Hines is the polished corporate face of moral evasion, the man who can say the right thing while standing directly inside the wrong thing. He’s not a villain in the theatrical sense; he’s the institutional enabler who keeps the machine moving while pretending to be above it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran actor do elegant, controlled damage — think Michael Stuhlbarg or John Slattery in a prestige drama. It’s a great showcase for subtext, denial, and corporate doublespeak.

lead_characters.name: Father Franklin
lead_characters.hook: Father Franklin is the calm, worldly religious authority who understands the supernatural stakes faster than the media people do. He gives the script a grounded spiritual counterpoint and a rare voice of procedural competence in the chaos.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a seasoned actor a quiet authority part in the vein of Mark Margolis or David Strathairn — the expert who arrives with real knowledge. It offers a restrained, memorable turn rather than a showy one.

casting_characteristics: One central lead with heavy dialogue and moral complexity
Multiple 40s-70s supporting roles with strong character specificity
Burn-scar makeup and physical continuity for Heather
Several roles require credible live-broadcast and documentary-style performance

notable_requirements: TV studio build with stage, control room, green room, hallway, office, electrical closet
Period dressing for 1990s broadcast and office environments

technical.vfx_details: Oily-green signal corruption, ghosting, spectral appearances, temperature/flicker effects, and final supernatural manifestations of Willie and Sasha.
technical.sfx_needs: Electric chair execution effects, water tank sequence, burns, blood, seizures, practical lighting failures, smoke/static, and body-contortion moments.

rights_flags.detail: The Carmichael Hour is an original fictional program, but the script directly references real-world talk-show history and named occult books within the story world.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a prestige horror-thriller for streaming-first or specialty theatrical launch.

budget.note: The core footprint is studio-bound and mostly interior, but the period 1990s build, electric-chair execution effects, water-tank sequence, burn makeup, and recurring supernatural VFX keep it above a simple contained-thriller spend.

casting.note: Vance has to carry charisma, menace, guilt, and breakdown across a long runtime, while Sasha, Serena, Heather, and Willie all need precise tonal control. The role is attractive, but it narrows the pool to actors who can sell both authority and collapse.

development.note: The script’s final-act reveal depends on the audience buying the moral logic of Vance’s buried ethical failure and the supernatural rules around the broadcast curse. The documentary/archive framing helps, but the mythology still has to stay legible under pressure.

comp_set.title: The Menu
comp_set.why_it_comps: A high-concept genre piece that weaponizes spectacle, audience complicity, and social critique in a contained premium lane.

comp_set.title: Late Night with the Devil
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the live-broadcast horror engine, period media texture, and the sense that a studio event is becoming a supernatural trap.

comp_set.title: The Ring
comp_set.why_it_comps: The cursed-media mechanism and investigative dread map cleanly onto this script’s signal-based possession logic.

comp_set.title: Talk to Me
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns a simple ritual into a viral, youth-culture-adjacent horror engine with strong escalation.

comp_set.title: Nightcrawler
comp_set.why_it_comps: The morally corrosive media protagonist and the critique of appetite-for-violence make this a close tonal and character-market neighbor.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige horror, media-satire thrillers, and morally compromised antiheroes.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, slightly male-leaning but viable with genre-forward women; strongest with viewers who respond to elevated horror and true-crime-adjacent media critique.

budget_tier.note: A mostly contained 1990s studio feature with moderate VFX, practical effects, period dressing, and a few signature set pieces.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building elevated-genre slates
specialty distributors looking for a conversation-starting horror title
indie financiers with appetite for contained high-concept genre
producer-directors in the media-satire horror lane
buyers seeking awards-adjacent genre with a strong lead role
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where genre is the delivery system for social critique and a star-making lead performance. The contained studio setting and period media texture make it financeable without needing tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is specific and expandable in theory, but there is no clear spinoff vector beyond this story’s central Vance/Willie confrontation.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project an immediate buyer-facing hook and a clean marketing sentence, which is half the battle in a crowded genre market. It’s the kind of premise that can sell a script, a package, and a trailer in the same breath.
strengths.evidence: The opening execution broadcast and the later primetime live episode make the show itself the horror device.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The lead role is a star trap
strengths.what_it_means: Vance is the kind of morally compromised, charismatic lead that can reset an actor’s lane and attract serious talent. That matters because the movie’s commercial ceiling rises sharply if the central performance becomes an event.
strengths.evidence: Vance’s public charisma, private guilt, and final confession on live television.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The studio becomes a haunted system
strengths.what_it_means: The script turns a TV set into a story engine with rules, hierarchy, and escalating consequences, which makes the world feel bigger than a single gimmick. Buyers respond to worlds that generate scenes, not just premises.
strengths.evidence: Control room, green room, stage, office, hallway, and electrical closet all become active pressure points.

strengths.what_it_means: The archival/interview structure gives the movie a built-in authenticity layer and helps the supernatural material feel earned rather than arbitrary. That makes the concept easier to pitch to both genre buyers and prestige-minded execs.
strengths.evidence: The 2025 interviews with Shawn, Serena, and Heather intercut with archival footage and reconstructions.

strengths.what_it_means: The script isn’t just about a curse; it’s about what happens when public appetite for punishment becomes a business model. That gives the movie thematic weight and makes it feel timely rather than merely nostalgic.
strengths.evidence: Vance’s televised executions, congressional testimony, and final confession that he chose spectacle over truth.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The finale is a genuine event
strengths.what_it_means: The ending is built to be discussed, argued over, and remembered, which is exactly what helps a genre title break out of its lane. A finale that forces a moral choice on live TV is a strong word-of-mouth engine.
strengths.evidence: Vance must choose between turning off the camera and preserving Serena, then is punished for choosing spectacle.

whats_special.headline: This is a premium horror-thriller with a real commercial spine: a star-making antihero role, a clean high-concept hook, and a contained studio footprint that keeps the budget in the indie lane. The script’s media-satire angle and documentary framing give it a distinctive package buyers can understand fast, while the finale promises the kind of ending that drives conversation and clicks.

items.detail: The opening is immediately compelling, but the occult-broadcast rules, the prison books, the green signal, and the Sasha/Willie reveal stack up over time rather than landing as one clean mechanism. That’s not a deal-breaker, but it means the buyer conversation will include how much explanation the audience needs before the final act pays off.

items.area: The runtime is carrying a lot of moving parts.
items.detail: You have a courtroom-crime setup, a media satire, a haunted-studio horror engine, a documentary frame, and a moral confession story all running at once. The material is rich, but it also means the script is asking the audience to track several tonal and narrative systems simultaneously.

items.area: The lead role narrows the casting pool.
items.detail: Vance has to be seductive, funny, monstrous, wounded, and finally broken without losing control of the frame. That’s a great role, but it is not a broad casting lane, and the project’s commercial upside is tied to landing someone who can command the room from page one.

items.area: The period build is not free.
items.detail: The late-1990s studio, broadcast, and newsroom texture is doing real work here, and the execution set pieces are not small: electric chair, water tank, burn effects, and recurring signal corruption. It’s still financeable, but the buyer will know this is not a cheap contained thriller.

items.area: The rights and clearance pass is real.
items.detail: The script names Jerry Springer, Morton Downey Jr., O.J. Simpson, JonBenet Ramsey, Manson, COPS, Nirvana, McDonald's, Tower Records, Blockbuster Video, and the New York Times. None of that kills the project, but it does mean legal and clearance work is not incidental.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is structural clarity versus ambition: the script is doing a lot, and the mythology takes time to fully lock. Add a lead role that demands a very specific star and a non-trivial period/clearance package, and this becomes a smart buy only if the packaging is strong.
